 8th Pay Commission Faces Higher Fitment Factor Test After DA Hits 63%
 By Ananya Sharma 
 October 29, 2026 
 0 
 Copy URL Facebook Linkedin X WhatsApp 
 The 8th Pay Commission’s salary calculations have become more demanding after the reported increase in dearness allowance (DA) for central government employees pushed the rate to 63% of basic pay. The immediate decision raises monthly earnings and creates arrears, but it also changes the baseline against which any future fitment factor will be measured.
 According to Aaj Tak Business, the Union Cabinet approved a 3 percentage-point increase in DA, effective from 1 July 2026. The corresponding dearness relief (DR) for pensioners was also raised by 3 percentage points to 63% of basic pension. The report said the decision would benefit about 48.54 lakh central government employees and 68.71 lakh pensioners.
 For households dependent on government salaries and pensions, the decision has two distinct effects. The first is immediate: monthly DA-linked income rises, with arrears payable for the period from July to October. The second is longer term: when the 8th Pay Commission reviews the existing pay structure, it will have to account for the larger portion of current pay already represented by DA.
 That distinction matters because a fitment factor is not the same as a real increase in purchasing power. The factor is used to convert an employee’s existing basic pay into a new basic pay under a future pay commission. When a new pay commission is implemented, the existing DA is generally absorbed into the revised basic pay and the DA rate begins again from a new base. As a result, part of the fitment factor merely replaces compensation that employees were already receiving through DA.
 The portion left after that adjustment represents the effective increase in basic pay. The higher the DA before the new pay structure is introduced, the larger the adjustment required simply to preserve the employee’s existing basic-plus-DA position. A larger headline fitment factor does not automatically translate into an equivalent increase in real income.
 The report used the 7th Pay Commission as the reference point for this calculation. The 7th Pay Commission came into effect from 1 January 2016, when central employees were receiving DA at 125%, according to the report. It said the commission fixed a fitment factor of 2.57, with 2.25 attributed to the adjustment of existing DA and the remaining portion associated with an effective salary increase of about 14%.
 The comparison is being made differently for the 8th Pay Commission because the current DA rate is reported at 63%. At this level, an employee’s basic pay plus DA is equal to 1.63 times the basic pay. A fitment factor below 1.63 could therefore produce a revised basic pay lower than the existing basic pay plus DA, before other components of the salary are considered.
 The report estimated that a fitment factor of about 1.86 would be required to deliver a real increase of roughly 14%, similar to the increase used in its comparison with the 7th Pay Commission. When DA was assumed to be 60%, the corresponding estimate was about 1.83. The three percentage-point rise in DA therefore raises the factor needed to preserve the same level of real salary growth.
 A Level-1 employee with a basic salary of ₹18,000 illustrates the difference between current income and future pay calculations. At 63% DA, the employee receives ₹11,340 as DA, taking basic pay plus DA to ₹29,340. At the earlier 60% rate, DA on the same basic pay was ₹10,800, making the monthly increase ₹540. For four months, the reported arrears would amount to ₹2,160.
 These figures do not represent total take-home salary. Actual monthly earnings will also depend on other allowances, deductions and the rules applicable to the employee. They also do not establish what the employee’s final salary would be under the 8th Pay Commission, because no fitment factor has been approved.
 The calculation becomes especially important in discussions around higher proposed factors such as 2.57, 2.86, 3.00 or 3.833. These numbers are being discussed as possible scenarios, but the report makes clear that they are not final figures approved by the government or the commission. Treating any of them as an announced pay decision would therefore be premature.
 The report also showed how the same fitment factor can produce a lower percentage increase when the starting DA is higher. At a factor of 1.86, the estimated real increase falls from about 16.3% when DA is 60% to about 14.1% when DA is 63%. At a factor of 2.57, the estimated increase falls from about 60.6% to 57.7%. The reported gap ranges from roughly 2.2 to 4.4 percentage points across the examples cited.
 This is the institutional issue at the centre of the debate: the government must separate inflation compensation from structural wage revision. DA is designed to respond to changes in the cost of living, while a pay commission reviews the broader pay architecture. If the two are combined without clearly identifying the adjustment component, a large fitment factor can appear to deliver a substantial increase even when much of it only absorbs existing DA.
 The financial scale is also significant. The reported annual combined cost of the latest DA and DR increase is about ₹10,016.10 crore. That expenditure affects the Union government’s salary and pension commitments, while also adding income to a large group of households. The decision therefore sits at the intersection of public finance, employee compensation and household purchasing power.
 The 8th Pay Commission was formed in November 2025, according to the report, and is chaired by retired Supreme Court Justice Ranjana Prakash Desai. It has been given 18 months to submit its report, which places the expected deadline around May 2027. The commission is currently consulting different stakeholders, but the report said no final decision has been taken on either the fitment factor or the revised salaries.
 A further change in DA could alter the calculation again. The report said that if DA rises by another 3 percentage points from January 2027 to reach 66%, a fitment factor of approximately 1.90 would be needed to achieve a real increase of around 14% under the same method. This is a calculation scenario, not an announced increase or an approved pay formula.
 For central employees and pensioners, the immediate outcome is the additional DA and the arrears linked to the July effective date. For the wider public, the more important question is how the 8th Pay Commission distinguishes inflation relief from genuine wage revision. The evidence currently establishes the new DA rate, its estimated beneficiaries and the financial cost, but not the final fitment factor or the eventual salary structure. Those decisions will depend on the commission’s recommendations and the government’s approval after its report is submitted.
